claims.text: Uncertainty quantification is challenging in applications of large language models that generate free-form responses.
Identifying task-specific uncertainties, such as semantic uncertainties, is difficult to define in general cases for free-form response generation.
This work addresses challenges in uncertainty quantification and calibration for natural language generation from a Bayesian decision theory perspective.
The utility is characterized by a similarity measure that compares a generated response with a hypothetical true response.
The assumption of utility characterized by a similarity measure enables principled quantification of the model's subjective uncertainty and its calibration.
A measure for epistemic uncertainty is derived based on a missing data perspective and characterized as an excess risk.
The proposed methods can be applied to black-box language models.
The methods are illustrated on question answering and machine translation tasks.
Experiments provide a principled evaluation of task-specific calibration.
Epistemic uncertainty offers a promising deferral strategy for efficient data acquisition in in-context learning.

evidence.description: Applications of large language models often involve the generation of free-form responses, in which case uncertainty quantification becomes challenging.
This is due to the need to identify task-specific uncertainties (e.g., about the semantics) which appears difficult to define in general cases.

This work addresses these challenges from a perspective of Bayesian decision theory, starting from the assumption that our utility is characterized by a similarity measure that compares a generated response with a hypothetical true response.

methodologies.name: Bayesian decision theory perspective for uncertainty quantification
methodologies.description: A framework for uncertainty quantification and calibration in NLG based on Bayesian decision theory, using a similarity measure for utility.
